newsitem.title: INDIA: India edible oil price continue to ease back.
newsitem.headline: India edible oil price continue to ease back.

text.p: Indian domestic edible oil prices eased further during the week as demand fell on the end of the marriage season and as arrivals of imported oils increased, traders said on Wednesday.
"Prices are falling due to lack of demand as the marriage season has ended, plus there is the pressure of imported oil," said C.M. Amla, a leading New Delhi edible oil trader.
Industry officials said about 15,000 tonnes of imported edible oil arrived at Bombay in the past week.
"Prices are softening every day as the monsoon has arrived and sowing for the new crop had started," said Navinbhai Shah, president of the Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange Ltd.
Shah said groundnut plantings had begun in some regions in the western state of Gujarat and the southern states of Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.
"Monsoon progress is slow but satisfactory in these regions," Shah said. "Sowing has started but only on a small scale."

Industry officials said domestic arrivals of the summer oilseed crop were over in all states except Gujarat. "About 40,000 bags of groundnut in shell was arriving in the Saurashtra region per day," Shah said.
One bag equals 70 kg. Saurashtra in Gujarat is the main groundnut growing region in the state.
Traders said groundnut oil was quoted at about 35,300-35,800 rupees per tonne, compared with 35,600 rupees last week. Palm olein traded at 26,500 rupees per tonne against 26,800 last week.
They said crude sunflower oil was quoted at 25,800 rupees in domestic markets.
Traders and industry officials said prices were expected to remain depressed until late August due to a lack of demand, but would start rising when the Hindu festival season started in September.
"For another two months prices will remain soft due to the lean period," Amla said. "After that prices will start rising as both festival and the marriage season begins."
September to November is the Hindu festival period when demand for edible oil rises sharply but domestic supply dries up, resulting in higher prices.
